text: 1 Communication by Dr/ Somaya Madkour Professor of Forensic Medicine & Clinical Toxicology Alexandria University 2 Communication ILOs ▪ Explain the differences between written and oral communication. ▪ List types of written communication in health care setting. ▪ Define nonverbal communication. ▪ Describe the main functions of nonverbal communication. ▪ List types of nonverbal communication. ▪ Describe each type. Communication is a process by which information is transferred or exchanged between people through a common system of symbols, signs, or behavior. In the medical field, the whole practice of medicine relies heavily on communication. It is done for, swapping of ideas, delivering messages, and exchanging information through signals, speech, or writings. • Seeing: Deliver 55% of the message. It is seen or felt and consists of facial expression, dress, grooming, posture, eye contact, touch, and gesture • Hearing: the heard voice that depends on the tone, vocal clarity, and verbal expressiveness. It delivers 38% of the message • The words by themselves delivering only 7% of the message Mark Twain, a famous American poet-writer, said, “If we were supposed to talk more than listen, we would have been given two mouths and one ear.” Doctors, while communicating with their patients, should master both the tongue and the body language. Usually, all forms of communication tools internally and externally are used while conducting a consultation. Having strong communication skills is essential for building both personal and professional relationships. There are two predominant types of communication: verbal and nonverbal. While most of us are aware of and use verbal communication on a regular basis, nonverbal communication is most commonly not intentional and can offer considerable information about both people and situations. Types of Communication 1. Verbal oral Communication Oral communication refers to the spoken words in the communication process. It can be a talk with or without illustrations. The audience listens and watches the verbal presentation of information given by the speaker. There are a large number of different verbal oral communication skills. They range from the obvious (being able to speak clearly, or listening, for example), to the more subtle (such as reflecting and clarifying). Examples of oral Communication ▪ Face-to-face conversation 3 ▪ Giving a speech (lecture & seminars) ▪ Telephonic conversation ▪ Sending voice note over the internet ▪ Taking interviews ▪ Group discussion in workplace ▪ Thesis defense Verbal communication skills There are basically two communication skills widely accepted. They are known as Effective speaking and active listening. • Effective speaking involves how well we choose our words. • Active listening involves how patiently we hear others. • These factors affect the transmission of messages. • Saves a lot of time and money. • These skills bring a positive response. Components of verbal communication • Pitch of the voice • Speed of the voice • Tone • Language • Grammar Advantages of oral Communication ▪ It saves a lot of time, money and energy. ▪ There are fewer chances of confusion because of clarity of method. ▪ The information conveyed in verbal communication is easy to understand, as the doubts are cleared immediately. ▪ Feedback is got quickly once a message is delivered. ▪ It is a very reliable form of communication and thus people prefer it worldwide over other types of communication. ▪ Verbal communication is the most convenient method of communication for its straightforward and understandable quality. ▪ Any person who can speak a language can easily communicate verbally and does not need any material to convey the messages. Disadvantages of Verbal Communication 1. Language differences – If the receiver is unaware of the sender’s language, then communication cannot be carried out. So, difference in language and dialect is a big barrier in the path of effective communication. 2. Lack of records – There is no means of recording the information permanently unless any modern device of storage is used. Hence, one cannot refer to the communication later on. 3. Unsuitable for long messages – When a lengthy message is to be imparted, then this form of communication is not at all suitable. The important points may be missed out and the lengthy paragraphs may cause misinterpretation by the receiver. 4. Communication-gap – While conveying messages orally several irrelevant and unimportant information may get included. This may cause a communication gap and thus retard the effectiveness of the communication. 4 5. No rectification – Speaking is a spontaneous process and several mistakes can happen in the process if not taken into consideration. There is no place for rectification once a message is sent. It is one way method. It is speaker centered! Rules of conveying messages orally The speaker has to be sure of five rules while conveying his message namely: 1. Clear (واضح:) • Use words and expressions that are clear to the ear! • Avoid expressions such as "The former", "the latter" and "respectively". • Allow questions from the responder to your message to ensure being understood. 2. Concise (few words) (مختصر:) • Use few words so that your important message will not be lost. (Less is more!) 3. Consistent (ثابت :) • State the message in a consistent and accurate manner all the time for all persons. Make the take home message persistent! 4. Credible/Reasonable (موثوق به /معقول:) • Make sure your message is real. Use reliable resources. Be particularly careful with internet sources. Remember, it is important that you mean what you say. 5. Courteous (Polite): • Always be polite and considerate in your wording. • Words and phrases such as: “hello", "thank you", "please", "excuse me" and "I' am sorry" are easy, effective ways to demonstrate respect. • Courtesy (politeness) is a must in the medical profession. Keep your personal feelings out of your work interactions. Avoid diminishing or embarrassing your listeners. 2. Verbal Written Communication The act of transferring and exchanging information through written letters, symbols, and words is called written communication. Written communication skills are one of the most important job skills an employee must have in any organization including health organization and health facilities. Example of Written Communication ▪ Letters and applications ▪ E-mails ▪ Memos and reports ▪ Bulletins and advertisements ▪ Brochures, handbills and leaflets ▪ Instant online messages ▪ Forms and questionnaires Advantages of Written Communication ▪ Permanent Record – The written documents can be recorded and stored permanently as proofs and evidences for future references. ▪ Accuracy – as there is a wide scope of repeated checking, and rectification ▪ Allows lengthy and complex communication – Long messages can be conveyed very easily through written communication. It also facilitates transmission of complex official orders, agendas, manuals, assignment of responsibilities and like. 5 ▪ Acceptability – The written form of information is accepted widely as it is considered authentic and removes any misunderstanding and conflict. ▪ Multitudinous and uniform approach – A large number of people can get information at the same time through written communication. Written document also ensures uniformity of the information sent to each and every person. ▪ Slow and steady process – Writing can be carried out slowly, carefully and consciously by checking and correcting the mistakes, unlike verbal communication which is more spontaneous and prone to errors. In this way, written communication becomes more effective than any other form of communication. ▪ Creative – Availability of more time enables the sender to employ creativity in their writing. This elevates the quality of communication, thus opening better and effective outcome. Disadvantages of Written Communication ▪ Time consuming – Compared to speaking, writing takes a lot of time and becomes more difficult for those who struggle with their writing proficiency. ▪ Not helpful for illiterate people – Illiterate people can neither read nor write. ▪ Lack of personal touch – Written form of communication is unable to display facial expressions, sentiments, emotions and tone of voice. Hence the messages cannot be obtained in its totality and may cause miscommunication. ▪ Delayed feedback – Feedback is a very important element of communication. It provides remarks to the senders which help them to gain confidence or understand the errors and drawbacks in the communication and do the needful adjustments. Unlike verbal communication, written communication lacks immediate feedback. ▪ Carelessness increases with length – As written communication generally includes detailed explanations and complete information so it becomes very lengthy. For this reason the receiver loses interest and tends to skim through the long paragraphs, thus missing important points. Written communication formats used in health services Written communication is used tremendously (بكثرة) in health care management. Written communication can come in many forms such as: a. Written notes between departments. b. Written communication between supervisors and employees c. Written instructions to health team members d. Patient discharge instructions. Now electronic communication is becoming standard practice. Example of these is: E-mails, Electronic lab results, Procedure and operative reports & Patient documentations. Utilities of written communication Written communication skills can help in: 1. Enhancing the image (تعزيز الصورة) of health services. 2. Laying down (إرساء) apparent principles, policies and rules for running the services. 3. Assisting in proper delegation (تفويض) of responsibilities. 4. Instructing health team and patients. 5. Improving reports of managerial issues and scientific research and findings. 6. Minimizing confusion. 6 7. Leading to better patient care. 8. Providing ready records and references. 9. Providing valid records for legal matters. 10. Determining the quality of healthcare delivery and life. Nonverbal communication Nonverbal communication is the transfer of information through the use of body language including eye contact, facial expressions, gestures and more. For example, smiling when you meet someone conveys friendliness, acceptance and openness. Everyone uses nonverbal communication all the time whether they know it or not. Nonverbal communication is dependent on seeing and analyzing physical movements as opposed to verbal communication, or the use of language to transfer information through written text, speaking or sign language. In order to understand body language and other aspects of non-verbal communication, we need to focus on our behavior during the conversation. Our body sends out signals (اشارات) no matter where we are, what we are doing or the time of the day. Our body does not know how to lie; it cannot “be turned off”. The most important thing in communication is hearing what is not said Functions of nonverbal communication (Relationship between Verbal and Non-verbal Communication) ▪ Repeating – using specific gestures to strengthen a verbal message (e.g. pointing to the object of discussion). ▪ Conflicting – when verbal and non-verbal messages within the same interaction send contradicting meaning. Conflicting messages often arise from feelings of confusion, indecision, or frustration (e.g. a friend saying how they had a great time during the party, but his voice sounds flat and his face lacks emotion). When action conflicts with verbal message, we tend to rely more on the nonverbal communication. Since much nonverbal communication is below our level of awareness, non-verbal clues are often harder to fade than verbal ones. ▪ Complementing – the accuracy of understanding information is greater when the nonverbal and verbal complement each other. Messages have been shown to be correctly recalled to a greater degree when body language affirms the verbal exchange (e.g. saying you are happy and joyfully showing it too). When we say ‘no’ and at the same time shake our head from side-to-side to reinforce the negative verbalization, we are complementing the verbal message. ▪ Substituting – at times non-verbal behaviour is used as the sole channel for communication. A simple gesture can substitute words (e.g. shaking your head to say no). When we nod our head up and down in approval of an action, we mean “yes” without using the word. Here we have substituted nonverbal sign for verbal sign. ▪ Regulating – we can use non-verbal signals to regulate speech. Called “turn-taking signals”, these gestures make it possible for us to alternate between speaking and listening (e.g. touching someone´s arm can signal that you want to talk next). ▪ Accenting – when we use non-verbal signals to emphasize our words. Good speakers will know when to use strong gestures, deliberate pauses, changes in vocal volume or speech 7 rate, etc. (e.g. someone who is verbally expressing anger may accent the message by speaking very loudly). Types on Non-Verbal Communication 1. Bodily movement 2. Touch 3. Paralanguage 4. Personal space 5. Time 6. Physical appearance 7. Silence 1- Bodily movement (facial expression, eye contact, posture, head movement and gestures) Facial expression The human face is expressive to a major extent. Through facial expressions, one can express various kinds of feelings, without saying a word. keeping an open warm fascial expression helps to build rapport with patients and colleagues. Ensure that your facial expression matches the content of your speech as this has a positive impact on building rapport, trust and confidence. Using the eyebrows, mouth, eyes and facial muscles to convey messages can be very effective when communicating both emotion and information. Unlike some forms of non-verbal communication, facial expressions are universal. The facial expressions for happiness, sadness, anger, worry, stress, anxiety, fear and surprise are the same for all the individuals, irrespective of their categories and backgrounds. You can interpret several behaviors by observing facial expressions. • An open expressions and mild smile can indicate respect. • Smiling and moistening lips may be interpreted as liking. • Hostility can be revealed by scowling (مقتطب الجبين/تجهم الوجه glaring (غاضبand clenched teeth. • Distress can be interpreted by rapid swallowing, rapid biting and wetting of lips as well as sadness expressions. Eye contact Of all the parts of the human body, the eyes are the most important for transmitting nonverbal information. Eyes are very expressive. They can reveal the inner feelings and emotions. Eye contact is frequently the first message before a spoken word. You can use eye contact to control a conversation. Example: • Looking away from someone and at the ground or your phone may convey disinterest or disrespect. • Making eye contact signals that you are listening and interested in what other person is saying. Be aware of culture differences. For example, in some cultures extended gaze convey hostility and rudeness • Eye open wide may mean amazement (surprise). • Frequent blinking may signal a fear reaction. • Pupil dilation, wide and narrowing eyes may be interpreted as liking. • Hostility can be revealed by glaring, rolling in disgust and averted gaze. 8 Posture The way you sit or stand or walk can give clues to feelings and emotions. The manner in which persons hold their bodies indicates their mood, their background and their willing to communicate. Example: • a slumped posture, can indicate tiredness. • shoulder relaxed with an upright posture, facing towards the other person indicates confidence and openness. • Leaning forward while facing the person demonstrates interest Head movement Head nod is a sign of acknowledgment. it can also be used to show that you are listening and encourage the patient to continue You can interpret several behaviors by observing head movements. • A head bow indicates respect. • A rapid nodding and tilting your head indicate liking. • Hostility can be revealed by shaking of head and tilting it. • Distress may also be revealed by shaking head. • Deceit can be interpreted by nodding when saying no and shaking the head when saying yes. Gestures While gestures vary widely across communities, they are generally used both intentionally and unintentionally to convey information to others. The word gesture refers to movement of arms and hands and occasionally the head and more rarely the whole body. Gestures serve to emphasize, clarify, or add to the verbal content of a message. Now how do we interpret gestures? • An increase in gestures suggests enthusiasm, pleasure and excitement. • Hand gestures may function as regulators in conversation. • Open hands with palms facing upwards or towards the other person suggest receptivity and respect. • Putting the thumps up: An-OK finger gestures indicate approval. • Scratching or rubbing face or nose and covering the mouth with a hand or crossing and uncrossing their legs all these may indicate stress and deceit. • Hiding hands behind one's back or sitting on the hands suggests shyness and insecurity. • Biting one's fingernails, squeezing tightly the hands or playing with a ring may be manifestations of nervousness, tension and embarrassment. • Sucking a thumb indicates stress and insecurity. • Fingertips planted spread apart on a surface display confidence and authority. • Arm spread out over chairs indicate that the person is feeling comfortable and confident. • Mirroring indicates liking. • Hostility can be revealed by shaking fists, crossed arms, hands on hips and pointing fingers. • Distress may also be revealed by hands around mouth, wringing hands (فرك اليدينjiggling legs (هزهزة الرجلand feet turned in, crossed arms and fidgeting (يعبثwith adornments حلى- سبحة).) • Leaning forward is a sign of acceptance. • Crossed feet may mean that the person is at ease. 9 • Feet tapping can indicate readiness to leave Patients, who are mechanically ventilated, are most likely to use head nods, and gestures as their primary methods of communication. 2- Touch Touching behavior is one of the most sensitive means of communication. It is described as an invisible communication system. This is because so much meaning may be transmitted by it independent of other senses. it conveys many messages and can be beneficial in giving the meaning of support and showing care and concern Example: Placing your hand on a friend’s shoulder may convey support or empathy. In situations of severe personal stress, particularly when the person feels isolated and threatened a touch can have comforting effects. Be aware of culture differences 3- Paralanguage: Vocal cues that accompany speech are called paralanguage (Para verbal communication). It is neither the language nor the signs used in communication. These cues may reveal an emotional state, attitudes towards others, social class, or origin. Paralanguage includes the non-language elements of speech, such as your talking pace, pitch, tone, volume and more. a. Pitch نبرة الصوت) :or intensity of speech. high pitch indicates feeling of joy, fear, and anger. a low pitch can indicate depression or state of calm. Women's voices are generally pitched higher than men. We may pitch our voice lower as a warning signal or as a defensive mechanism. We can lower our pitch along with the volume when we want to establish more intimate communication, or to show respect. We tend to pitch our voice higher with people we know. Changes in pitch reflect changes in emotion. Sudden shift to high pitch may reflect excitement. b. Volume: loudness can indicate confidence or aggression. soft voice can indicate helplessness or gentleness c. Pace: refers to how fast or slow a person speak s. Fast talker can convey excitement or nervousness while slow voice can indicate indifference or thoughtful. d. Tone: is the most complex vocal character. Pleasing voice are generally those that are lower in pitch and not monotone Vocal cues are associated with culture. In Arab culture, for example, speaking loudly indicates sincerity, whereas in North America it often is interpreted as aggressiveness. Voice expressions may denote different behaviors: • It can reflect respect by being silent. • It may indicate liking where the voice will have a higher pitch and warmer tone. • Hostility may be revealed with loud voice and deeper pitch. • Distress and deceit could be diagnosed by vocal cues where in both conditions one can observe shaking voice, non -words, partial words, repetitions, stumbling over words (تعثر الكلماتand higher pitch 4- Personal space: Creating or closing distance between yourself and the people around you can also convey messages about your comfort level, the importance of the conversation, your desire to support or connect with others and more. We tend to feel anxious if others invade this space; by standing too close or by touching us. There are four zones that are identified 10 a) Public zone: is 12-20 feet from the body. the communication that occurs in this zone is formal like a teacher in the classroom, within this zone we will also be comfortable with people we know only slightly or we do not at all. b) Social zone: 4-12 feet from the body. This is preferred zone for a professional interaction as it reduces the suggestion of inappropriate behavior or unintentional touching. Also for people we know only moderately well as work colleagues in a meeting. c) Personal zone: 1.5-4 feet from the body. this is the zone for friends, people we know well. and health care workers. You can easily touch the person and discuss issues in relative privacy d) Intimate zone: 0-1.5 feet from the body. this is allowed for close friends and loved ones. Being close to someone and feeling their physical presence can be very comforting when words fail. 5- Time: ovoid glancing at the clock during consultation. It suggests that you wish to finish the conversation 6- Physical appearance • Appearance messages are generally the first nonverbal messages received. • They can be used to develop judgments about people based on how they look, what they wear, and their level of attractiveness. • Your physical appearance will help you to present yours elf to others ( self- presentation). • A tall person appears to command more attention and trust than a short one • Your appearance, color, clothes, hairstyle, cosmetics and accessories may give several messages to receivers. 7- Silence: As a student of medicine, you must recognize and respect individual differences in the way they respond. The quiet person, the person with a language barrier or speech problem, the elderly and persons who lack confidence in their ability to communicate all these may resort to silence. Silence is a specific channel for transmitting and receiving messages. Silence may suggest: • Intimacy. • Evaluating and judging another's words. • Drawing attention to certain ideas or words. • Anxiety. • Fear of disclosure. • Emotional blocking and sadness. • Anger and hostility. Student’ learning outcomes at the end of the session, you will be able to 2 Communication is a process by which information is transferred or exchanged between people through a common system of symbols, signs, or behavior. In the medical field, the whole practice of medicine relies heavily on communication. It is done for, swapping of ideas, delivering messages, and exchanging information through signals, speech, or writings. 3 • Seeing: Deliver 55% of the message. It is seen or felt and consists of facial expression, dress, grooming, posture, eye contact, touch, and gesture. •Hearing: the heard voice that depends on the tone, vocal clarity, and verbal expressiveness. It delivers 38% of the message. •The words by themselves delivering only 7% of the message. Types of communication Verbal Oral Written Non-Verbal There are basically two communication skills widely accepted. They are known as Effective speaking and active listening. •Effective speaking involves how well we choose our words. •Active listening involves how patiently we hear others. •These factors affect the transmission of messages. •Saves a lot of time and money. •These skills bring a positive response. Components of verbal communication: •Pitch of the voice. •Speed of the voice. •Tone. •Language. •Grammar. 5 Item of comparison Oral Written Example Face-to-face conversation. Giving a speech (lecture & seminars). Telephonic conversation. Sending voice note over the internet. Taking interviews. Group discussion in workplace. Thesis defense. Letters and applications. E-mails. Memos and reports. Bulletins and advertisements. Brochures, handbills and leaflets. Instant online messages. Forms and questionnaires. It is one way method. It is speaker centered! Written communication formats used in health services. 6 Advantages Disadvantages Oral Save a lot of time, money and energy. Fewer chances of confusion because it is clear method . The information is easy to understand as doubts are cleared immediately . Feedback is got quickly once a message is delivered. It is a very reliable form of communication .It is preferred worldwide Any person who can speak a language can easily communicate verbally and does not need any material to convey the messages. Language differences – If the receiver is unaware of the sender’s language difference in language Lack of records – There is no means of recording unless any modern device of storage is used. Unsuitable for long messages –The important points may be missed out and the lengthy paragraphs may cause misinterpretation by the receiver. Communication-gap – as several irrelevant and unimportant information may get included. This may cause a communication gap and thus retard the effectiveness of the communication. No rectification – Speaking is a spontaneous process and several mistakes can happen in the process if not taken into consideration. 7 Rules of conveying messages orally Clear. Avoid expressions such as "The former", "the latter" and "respectively". Allow questions from the responder to your message to ensure being understood. Concise (few words). Consistent ( accurate manner all the time and for all person Credible/Reasonable( the message is real one, use reliable resources . Be cautious with the internet sources ) . Courteous (Polite). Use words like please, hello, thank you 8 Advantages Disadvantages Verbal Written communication Permanent Record – The written documents can be recorded and stored permanently as proofs Accuracy – repeated checking, and rectification Allows lengthy and complex communication – It facilitates transmission of complex official orders, agendas, assignment . Acceptability – The written form of information is accepted widely as it is removes any misunderstanding and conflict. Multitudinous and uniform approach – A large number of people can get information at the same time through written communication. Written document also ensures uniformity of the information sent to each and every person. Slow and steady process – it can be carried out slowly, carefully by checking and correcting the mistakes, unlike verbal communication which is more spontaneous and prone to errors. In this way, written communication becomes more effective than any other form of communication. Time consuming –writing takes a lot of time Not helpful for illiterate people Lack of personal touch – Written form of communication is unable to display facial expressions, emotions and tone of voice. Delayed feedback –Unlike verbal communication, written communication lacks immediate feedback. Carelessness increases with length – it is very lengthy so the receiver loses interest and tends to skim through the long paragraphs, thus missing important points. 9 Non-Verbal communication Everyone uses nonverbal communication all the time whether they know it or not. Our body sends out signals no matter where we are, what we are doing or the time of the day. Our body does not know how to lie; it cannot “be turned off”. The most important thing in communication is hearing what is not said. Functions of nonverbal communication (Relationship between Verbal and Non-verbal Communication) Repeating – using specific gestures to strengthen a verbal message (e.g. pointing to the object of discussion). Conflicting-When action conflicts with verbal message, we tend to rely more on the nonverbal communication. Complementing-Messages have been shown to be correctly recalled to a greater degree when body language affirms the verbal exchange. Substituting – at times non-verbal behaviour is used as the sole channel for communication. (e.g. shaking your head to say no). Regulating – we can use non-verbal signals to regulate speech. Called “turn-taking signals” . listening (e.g. touching someone´s arm can signal that you want to talk next). Accenting – when we use non-verbal signals to emphasize our words. B) Eye contact : Eyes are very expressive. They can reveal the inner feelings and emotions. .Eye contact is frequently the first message before a spoken word. Example: • Looking away from someone and at the ground or your phone may convey disinterest or disrespect. • Eye open wide may mean amazement (surprise). • Frequent blinking may signal a fear reaction. •Hostility can be revealed by glaring, rolling in disgust and averted gaze.
